record.paper_title: Some Open Problems Related to Creative Telescoping
record.original_question: Design an algorithm that takes as input a nonzero recurrence operator P ∈ Q[n][S_n] and, when possible, finds a bivariate hypergeometric term f(n, k) for which P is a telescoper, meaning that there exists a certificate operator Q with P − (S_k − 1)Q annihilating f.

evidence.quote: Problem 8.1 Design an algorithm which takes as input a nonzero recurrence operator P ∈ Q[n][Sn] and finds, if at all possible, a bivariate hypergeometric term f(n, k) which has P as a telescoper.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{Q}[n][S_n]$ denote the Ore algebra of linear recurrence operators in the shift operator $S_n$ (acting by $S_n\cdot a(n) = a(n+1)$) with coefficients in $\mathbb{Q}[n]$. A bivariate sequence $f(n,k)$ is called a (bivariate) hypergeometric term if both ratios $f(n+1,k)/f(n,k)$ and $f(n,k+1)/f(n,k)$ are rational functions of $n$ and $k$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Given a nonzero operator $P \in \mathbb{Q}[n][S_n]$, we say that $P$ is a telescoper for a hypergeometric term $f(n,k)$ if there exists a rational function $Q$ (the certificate, viewed as an operator in $\mathbb{Q}(n,k)[S_k]$) such that
\[
\bigl(P - (S_k - 1)Q\bigr)\, f(n,k) = 0.
\]

Design an algorithm with the following specification: it takes as input a nonzero recurrence operator $P \in \mathbb{Q}[n][S_n]$, and outputs either
(i) a bivariate hypergeometric term $f(n,k)$ (presented through its rational shift ratios) such that $P$ is a telescoper for $f$, together with an associated certificate $Q$, or
(ii) a proof that no such hypergeometric term exists.

Equivalently: characterize and effectively decide the image of the map sending a hypergeometric term to its minimal telescoper in $\mathbb{Q}[n][S_n]$, and provide a constructive inverse on this image.
artifact.status_search_result: This inverse problem for creative telescoping is listed as an open problem in surveys on creative telescoping. Web search returns only the original problem listing and related works on the forward direction (reduction-based telescoping, bounds for telescopers); no algorithm solving the inverse problem in this generality appears to have been published as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: The ABC of Creative Telescoping
status_evidence.snippet: We could ask whether a given recurrence admits a solution that can be expressed as a definite sum. In a way, this would be the inverse problem of creative telescoping.
status_evidence.claim: The inverse problem is discussed as an open research direction, with no general algorithm given.
